inputs._about: Inputs of the GM's Boeing balance-sheet tracker (finance.py) for Control's objective 'repair the balance sheet: debt back to historical levels'. Debt is NET debt (total debt minus cash and short-term investments), the measure both broker models and the S&P Capital IQ consensus forecast on a consistent basis. Money in $B, constant 2026 dollars (nominal figures deflated at the engine board's 2.2% CPI). Objective scoring only: the board's ΔPV and its own debt penalty on $45B of gross debt are unchanged.

sources.start: End-2026E net debt $22.53B: S&P Capital IQ consensus mean (TheBoeingCompanyNYSEBAEstimatesReport.xls, Consensus 'Net Debt', 5 estimates); GS $22.55B (GoldmanSachs_BA72826_Jul_30_2026.xlsx BS row 64), MS $23.01B (341995.BA.N.XLSM Balance_Sheet_Annual 'Net Debt'). Gross debt at 2Q26A $45.9B (both models), the board's $45B.
sources.base_fcf: Free cash flow 2027E-2030E, S&P Capital IQ consensus mean (Consensus 'Free Cash Flow'): $5.67B, $9.86B, $13.03B, $15.04B nominal (14, 10, 4 and 3 estimates). MS: 6.20, 10.33, 10.84, 12.76; GS: 6.51, 10.54, 13.64, 16.65. Held flat in real terms after 2030 (no broker forecast beyond 2030-31). None of these includes a new airplane programme.
sources.historical: Net debt 2010A-2018A (GS BS row 64, one definition throughout): 1.90, 1.10, -3.15, -5.62, -4.02, -2.09, -0.08, 1.13, 5.28; mean -$0.62B (a small net cash). Gross debt averaged $11.0B (range $9.1-13.8B).
sources.validation: With base cash flow only, the tracker gives net debt of $16.49B at end-2027 and $6.70B at end-2028 in 2026 dollars, against consensus $16.94B and $7.21B nominal, which is $16.57B and $6.90B in 2026 dollars; it reaches zero in 2029 (MS has -$3.6B in 2029E). The stress case reaches zero in 2030.
sources.capital_allocation: Debt first: every dollar of free cash flow goes to net debt until it is back at the historical level; after that surplus cash goes to the owners. MS models no buybacks to 2030 (net cash $16.2B in 2030E); GS models $42B of buybacks in 2027E-2030E (net debt $17.4B in 2030E). Boeing's Board reserves shareholder returns for itself until the rating is solid.
sources.stress: Stress case: base free cash flow one-third below consensus in every year. The lowest 2027E-2030E estimates are 79-92% of the mean (4.50, 7.99, 11.93, 13.34), but Boeing's record is worse: consensus 2026 free cash flow was cut from $5.05B to $2.15B (-57%) in twelve months (Trends sheet), and 2019-2025 free cash flow was negative in five of seven years.
sources.tax_rate: 21%, the US federal corporate rate, applied to the game's profit change after deducting programme spend (one treatment for both; Boeing's tax losses carried forward could shield both).
sources.real_rate: 3% real on debt the game adds: about 5% nominal (Boeing's 2025 interest of $2.77B on $54.1B of debt is 5.1% [MS BA Income_Statement_Annual r37, Balance_Sheet_Annual 'Total Debt']) less the 2.2% CPI.
sources.phasing_curve: A standard development-spend curve: light concept years, a peak at test-aircraft build, tapering through certification (5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 14, 13, 11, 9% of the bill over ten years), stretched to each programme's length. GM assumption; the analyst models have no new-programme phasing.
sources.cpi: 2.2% a year, the engine board's CPI: deflates consensus cash flow to 2026 dollars and erodes the real value of the debt stock. The airframer board's flows are unescalated 2026 prices and enter as they are.

inputs.historical_label: rounded from its 2010-2018 average of about -$0.6B, a small net cash
inputs.method_short: Net debt is total debt minus cash and short-term investments, in 2026 dollars. It starts at the consensus end-2026 figure ($22.5B) and falls each year by free cash flow: the analysts' consensus to 2030 (held flat after), plus 79% of (the profit the game adds or takes away against its baseline, less your programme cash as it is spent), less 3% real interest on any debt the game adds; the debt stock also loses 2.2% a year to inflation. Programme cash is each bill spread over its development years on a standard curve (5% in year 1 of 10, peaking at 14% in year 7), not at entry into service as the board books it; the 737 rate increase is spent evenly from the order to 2032 and adds profit from 2032; the board's two-front strain is spread over the years the fps and 787 Re-engine developments overlap. Years already played stay as played. Debt comes first: once net debt is back at the historical level, surplus cash goes to the owners. The stress case runs the same path with base free cash flow one-third lower.
